title: Design a web crawler.
description: Crawl frontier at scale: politeness, URL deduplication, fetch-scheduling architecture, content storage, and trap avoidance.

data.text: **Question:** Design a web crawler that can fetch and index a large portion of the web.

data.title: Functional Requirements
items: Start from seed URLs, discover new links by fetching and parsing pages
Polite crawling: respect robots.txt, per-domain rate limits, identifiable user agent
Never fetch the same URL twice (URL normalization + dedup)
Prioritize: important/fresh pages crawled more often than obscure ones
Robust against traps: infinite calendars, generated URLs, redirect loops
Persist raw content for downstream indexing pipelines

data.caption: Distributed crawler: frontier, fetchers, parsers, and dedup store
data.definition:
graph TD
    A[Seed URLs] --> B[(Frontier Queue - Kafka)]
    B --> C[Fetcher Pool 1]
    B --> D[Fetcher Pool 2]

    C --> F[(Content Store - S3/Blob)]
    C --> G[Parser Workers]
    G --> H{URL seen?}
    H -->|No| B

    K[Politeness Scheduler - per-domain queues] --> B
    L[robots.txt Cache] --> C

data.text: The core loop is fetch → store → parse → extract links → dedup → enqueue. Scale comes from the **frontier** (a durable queue, typically Kafka) feeding thousands of stateless fetchers, and from **sharding by domain** so politeness and ordering are enforceable per host.

items: URL normalization before dedup: lowercase host, strip fragments, resolve redirects, sort query params, collapse default ports — else the same page is fetched many times
Dedup at two levels: probabilistic (Bloom filter, billions of URLs, tiny memory — false positives acceptable) + exact KV store for confirmed URLs
Frontier design: per-domain queues (politeness) inside a global priority queue (importance); a domain's queue wakes on its next allowed fetch time
Politeness: max N concurrent fetches per domain, delay between requests, honor robots.txt Crawl-delay; cache robots.txt per domain with TTL
Prioritization: PageRank/link depth, content freshness, update frequency history, sitemap hints; re-crawl policy differs from discovery policy
Trap avoidance: URL-length/param-count limits, path-depth caps, per-domain discovered-URL budgets, redirect-hop limits, pattern detection (calendars with incrementing dates)
Content store: raw HTML blobs in object storage (cheap, durable) keyed by content hash; metadata (URL, fetch time, headers, hash) in a KV/relational store for the index pipeline
Failure handling: fetch failures retry with backoff (respect 429/Retry-After and 503); permanent 404s tombstoned; soft-404 detection via content heuristics
Parser scale-out: parsing/extracting is CPU-bound — separate worker pool from I/O-bound fetchers; dedup check happens before enqueue to keep the frontier small

data.title: The frontier is the whole design
data.text: A naive single queue produces both impoliteness (10k URLs from one site back-to-back) and starvation (small sites never reached). Sharding the frontier per domain with priority scheduling is what makes a crawler both fast and a good citizen — everything else is plumbing around that decision.

items: Infinite URL spaces (calendars, session-id URLs) — budget and pattern caps per domain
Redirect chains and cross-domain redirects — resolve, normalize, and re-apply politeness to the final domain
Duplicate content at different URLs — content hashing lets the indexer canonicalize
robots.txt changing mid-crawl — TTL cache with fail-closed on fetch error for disallowed paths
Politeness vs freshness tension for news sites — higher crawl rates for high-churn domains, with their permission
Legal/ToS boundaries: rate limits, copyrighted content storage policy — a design constraint, not an afterthought

items.question: How do you handle JavaScript-rendered pages?
items.answer: A headless-browser pool (Playwright/Chromium) for URLs flagged as JS-heavy — 10-100x costlier than HTTP fetch, so only a fraction of traffic goes through it; or rely on the site's own prerendering/sitemaps.

items.question: How does re-crawling differ from discovery?
items.answer: Discovery explores unknown URLs; re-crawling polls known pages based on observed change frequency. Track per-URL content-hash history and adapt intervals — stable pages get longer gaps, news pages get minutes.

items.question: Where does Kafka fit vs a custom queue?
items.answer: Kafka gives durable, replayable, partitioned throughput; the per-domain politeness layer sits on top (scheduler), since Kafka partitioning alone doesn't provide rate shaping.

items.question: How do you measure crawler health?
items.answer: Frontier depth, fetch success rate by class (2xx/3xx/4xx/5xx/timeout), pages/day per fetcher, dedup hit rate, average robots-blocked ratio, and parse-pipeline lag.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Frontier sharded by domain: politeness and priority scheduling in one design
Normalize + dedup (Bloom + exact KV) before enqueue
Fetchers (I/O) and parsers (CPU) scale separately; content in object storage
Trap budgets, robots.txt, and retry semantics are first-class components
data.takeaway: A crawler is a scheduling problem wearing a networking costume — the frontier's per-domain politeness and priority design decides whether you're a search engine or a menace.
